site.name: Eldora / Happy Valley–Eldorado Mining Camp & Historic District
site.componentDetail: Historic mining camp and National Register historic district
overview: Eldora grew from the Happy Valley mining camp during the early 1890s and became one of Boulder County's late Front Range mining booms.

The camp developed around gold and telluride mining in the Eldora–Grand Island district. By the late 1890s it had stores, hotels, an assay office, a chlorination mill, saloons, residences and other services supporting the surrounding mines.
The surviving community includes the Eldora Historic District. Respect private property and historic structures, and use public roads and legal access points.

timeline.text: John H. Kemp and partners located the Happy Valley Placer, helping trigger renewed prospecting in the area.
Important discoveries including the Bird's Nest, Village Belle and Enterprise helped accelerate the mining boom.
The camp's name was shortened from Eldorado to Eldora to avoid confusion with another Eldorado.
Eldora incorporated; the mining boom was near its height and the valley population reached roughly 2,500, with about 1,000 residents in Eldora.
The Bailey chlorination mill began operating under the Eldora Mining and Milling Company.

moreHistory: Boulder County's historic context describes Eldora as a mining camp that began in the early 1890s after the Happy Valley placer and nearby lode discoveries. Its boom produced a substantial service town for mines on Spencer Mountain and elsewhere in the district.
A period account identified Eldora as a principal camp of the district and a rail terminal where ores from the surrounding country were brought for shipment.
